specPoints.text: draw and explain energy level diagrams to represent exothermic and endothermic reactions

primer.text: From Exothermic & Endothermic you already know which reactions warm their surroundings and which cool them. This note draws that story as a picture, placing reactants and products on an energy axis so the direction of change can be read at a glance. Two carefully labelled sketches are all the exam asks for.

lessons.title: Reading the axes and arrows
lessons.opening: An energy level diagram is a map of where the energy sits before and after a reaction. This lesson fixes the axes, the two levels and the arrow that tells you which way the heat flowed.
keyPoints: An energy level diagram sets the energies of reactants and products side by side for comparison.
Energy runs up the y-axis while the x-axis tracks how far the reaction has progressed.
Arrows point downwards for exothermic reactions and upwards for endothermic ones.
The height difference between reactants and products represents the overall enthalpy change.
Reactants sit above products in exothermic reactions and below them in endothermic ones.

low.restatement: The sketch puts energy up the side and the run of the reaction along the bottom. Two lines mark the starting and ending energy, and an arrow between them shows heat leaving or entering.
low.analogy: It is like a thumbnail sketch of a hill walk: the two heights matter, and the arrow between them says whether you climbed or descended.
low.examPointer: Label both axes, both energy levels and the arrow direction whenever you draw or read one.

medium.restatement: The y-axis carries the energy of the reactants and products while the x-axis tracks the progress of the reaction. A downward arrow marks an exothermic change and an upward arrow an endothermic one, with the vertical gap giving the overall enthalpy change.
medium.analogy: Think of a lift journey between two floors: the shaft is the axis, the floors are the energy levels, and the direction of travel is the arrow.
medium.examPointer: Quote both features examiners scan for: labelled axes and a correctly directed arrow between the levels.

check.stem: What is plotted on the y-axis of an energy level diagram?

options.text: The energy of the reactants and products
options.explanation: The vertical axis carries the energy levels whose gap gives the enthalpy change.

options.text: The progress of the reaction
options.explanation: Progress runs along the x-axis; energy sits on the y-axis.

options.text: The temperature of the mixture
options.explanation: Temperature belongs to thermometer readings, not to this diagram.

options.text: The rate of the reaction
options.explanation: Rate graphs are a different topic with different axes.

check.stem: Which arrow direction marks an endothermic reaction on an energy level diagram?

options.text: Upwards, because the products end higher than the reactants
options.explanation: Energy taken in leaves the products on a higher level, so the arrow climbs.

options.text: Downwards, because the mixture cools
options.explanation: The cooling of the surroundings is not what the arrow tracks; the product level is higher.

options.text: Horizontal, because energy is conserved
options.explanation: Conservation governs total energy, not the levels drawn for the chemicals.

options.text: It depends on the temperature of the room
options.explanation: The arrow follows the chemistry, not the surroundings.

check.stem: What does the vertical gap between the reactant and product levels represent?

options.text: The overall enthalpy change of the reaction
options.explanation: The height difference is exactly the energy change the diagram is built to show.

options.text: The activation energy of the reaction
options.explanation: Activation energy appears on reaction profiles, not on simple energy level diagrams.

options.text: The time the reaction takes
options.explanation: Time never appears on an energy level diagram.

options.text: The temperature rise recorded by a thermometer
options.explanation: Thermometer data is experimental; the gap is the energy difference.

check.stem: In an exothermic energy level diagram, where do the products sit?

options.text: Below the reactants, because energy was given out
options.explanation: Released energy leaves the products on a lower level than the reactants.

options.text: Above the reactants, because the mixture warmed
options.explanation: Warming the surroundings does not lift the product level; giving out energy lowers it.

options.text: On the same level as the reactants
options.explanation: Equal levels would mean no enthalpy change at all.

options.text: Off the diagram, because products are unstable
options.explanation: Products sit firmly on their own level however stable they are.

check.stem: A diagram shows the product level above the reactant level. What does it depict?

options.text: An endothermic reaction with a positive enthalpy change
options.explanation: Higher products mean energy was taken in, which is the endothermic signature.

options.text: An exothermic reaction with a negative enthalpy change
options.explanation: Exothermic reactions place products lower, not higher.

options.text: A reaction with no energy change
options.explanation: A level difference always signals an energy change.

options.text: An incomplete reaction waiting for more energy
options.explanation: The diagram describes the energy bookkeeping, not the completion state.

lessons.title: Drawing the two labelled sketches
lessons.opening: The exam rewards two tidy sketches: one with products below reactants, one with products above. This lesson sets out the labels that must never be missing and the negatives that must never creep in.
keyPoints: An exothermic sketch shows reactants high, products low and a downward arrow between them.
An endothermic sketch shows reactants low, products high and an upward arrow between them.
Both sketches need labelled axes, named energy levels and the direction of energy change.
The enthalpy change is negative for the exothermic sketch and positive for the endothermic one.
Energy is given out in exothermic reactions and taken in in endothermic reactions.

low.restatement: Draw the axes first, then two levels: high-to-low with a down arrow for warming reactions, low-to-high with an up arrow for cooling ones. Write the names on every line.
low.analogy: Two sketches are like before-and-after photos on a staircase: the same stairs, but the people stand on different steps.
low.examPointer: Examiners award marks for labels, so annotate axes, levels and arrows before anything else.

medium.restatement: For the exothermic sketch place the reactant level above the product level and mark the change negative with a downward arrow. For the endothermic sketch reverse the placement, mark the change positive and point the arrow upwards.
medium.analogy: It is like drawing water slides in opposite directions: same structure, but one drops and one would need a pump to climb.
medium.examPointer: Pair each sketch with its sign: negative below, positive above, and keep the arrow obeying the same rule.

check.stem: Which set of features must every energy level diagram carry?

options.text: Labelled axes, named energy levels and a directed arrow
options.explanation: Those three elements let the reader extract the reaction type and the enthalpy change.

options.text: A curve through the transition state
options.explanation: Curves and peaks belong to reaction profiles, not energy level diagrams.

options.text: Time intervals along the x-axis
options.explanation: The x-axis carries reaction progress, not time.

options.text: The temperature values measured
options.explanation: Experimental temperatures are not part of the diagram.

check.stem: What sign belongs to the enthalpy change in the sketch with products below reactants?

options.text: Negative, because energy left the chemicals
options.explanation: A drop in level means energy was released, which is written as a negative change.

options.text: Positive, because the products are stable
options.explanation: Stability is not the sign rule; the direction of energy flow is.

options.text: Zero, because the arrow is short
options.explanation: Arrow length is a drawing choice, not the sign.

options.text: The sign depends on the fuel used
options.explanation: The placement of the levels fixes the sign whatever the chemicals.

check.stem: A student draws an exothermic diagram but points the arrow upwards. What should be corrected?

options.text: The arrow, which must point downwards from reactants to products
options.explanation: Exothermic changes lose energy, so the arrow descends to the lower product level.

options.text: Nothing: exothermic arrows point upwards
options.explanation: Upward arrows mark endothermic changes only.

options.text: The axes, which should swap places
options.explanation: The axes are correct; only the arrow direction is wrong.

options.text: The reaction type, which must be endothermic
options.explanation: The student intends an exothermic sketch; the drawing, not the intent, needs fixing.

check.stem: Why does the endothermic sketch carry a positive enthalpy change?

options.text: Energy is taken in, so the products end with more energy than the reactants
options.explanation: Gaining energy raises the product level and gives the change its positive sign.

options.text: Because the thermometer reads a higher number
options.explanation: Endothermic reactions make the thermometer fall; the sign comes from the energy flow.

options.text: Because the products are heavier
options.explanation: Mass has no role in the energy levels.

options.text: Positive signs are used for all sketches
options.explanation: Exothermic sketches are negative by the same convention.

check.stem: How can you identify the reaction type from a finished, labelled diagram?

options.text: Compare the reactant and product levels and note the arrow direction
options.explanation: Relative levels plus arrow direction give the type immediately.

options.text: Measure the length of the x-axis
options.explanation: The x-axis carries progress and its length means nothing.

options.text: Count the labels written on the diagram
options.explanation: Label count is a quality check, not a type test.

options.text: Check whether the diagram is drawn in pencil
options.explanation: Drawing medium has no chemical meaning.

glossary.definition: A sketch showing the relative energies of reactants and products, with energy on the y-axis and reaction progress on the x-axis.
The difference in height between the reactant and product energy levels.
The starting chemicals, drawn on their own energy level at the left of the diagram.
The finishing chemicals, drawn on their own energy level at the right of the diagram.
The horizontal axis quantity showing how far the reaction has run from start to finish.

workedExample.prompt: a) Describe the energy level diagram of an exothermic reaction. b) Describe the energy level diagram of an endothermic reaction. c) The combustion of methane is exothermic — state where its products sit relative to its reactants and the sign of the enthalpy change.
steps: a) Energy is plotted on the y-axis and reaction progress on the x-axis; the reactant level is drawn high and the product level low, with a downwards arrow between them showing energy given out.
b) The same axes are used, but the reactant level sits low and the product level high, with an upwards arrow showing energy taken in; the enthalpy change is positive.
c) In an exothermic reaction the products sit below the reactants (their energy is lower), so the enthalpy change is negative.
workedExample.finalAnswer: a) Reactants high, products low, downward arrow. b) Reactants low, products high, upward arrow, ΔH positive. c) Products below reactants; ΔH negative.
